articles.title: Two critical PHP flaws trigger global alert; millions of services face cyber risk
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Two critical PHP vulnerabilities that could allow hackers to remotely execute code on servers without authentication have triggered a
articles.body: BENGALURU: Two critical PHP vulnerabilities that could allow hackers to remotely execute code on servers without authentication have triggered a cybersecurity alert, potentially exposing millions of internet-facing services. In a separate advisory, PHP also urged users to temporarily disable a file-upload tracking feature to mitigate another remote code execution risk, adding to concerns over the widely used programming language.PHP advised users on Oct 23 to temporarily disable its session upload progress feature until the next regular bugfix release. The warning followed an earlier advisory on Oct 21 about a related vulnerability. The latest issue affects applications only when specific session settings are changed while running and the upload progress feature remains enabled. Users who have already disabled the feature do not need to take further action.The broader concerns centre on two critical vulnerabilities collectively referred to as PHP2Shell. Aamir Lakhani, global director of threat intelligence and adversarial artificial intelligence research at Fortinet, said: “Two critical PHP vulnerabilities disclosed this week pose an urgent security and business continuity risk for organizations that depend on websites, customer portals, and other web applications.”PHP is a server-side programming language used by widely deployed platforms such as WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento. Companies can be exposed through commercial applications, hosting providers and embedded software components even if they do not develop PHP applications themselves.The potential scale of exposure is significant. Censys identified approximately 36.7 million internet-facing services reporting potentially affected PHP versions in its Oct 22 snapshot. These are service counts, not unique servers or organisations, and may include installations already patched through vendor updates.Saeed Abbasi, head of the Threat Research Unit and director of product at Qualys, said the company found 167 million PHP package installations across 12,000 organisations, with 73% deployed on internet-facing assets, putting them within reach of remote attackers. “Applying a patch alone will not be sufficient for systems running unsupported versions, where upgrading is the only viable long-term solution. The key takeaway is that nearly all PHP installations are either vulnerable or running unsupported versions,” he said.CloudSEK said Shodan identified 2.2 million internet-facing services displaying PHP information worldwide, with India ranking ninth at 53,400 services. Of 36,700 Indian services revealing their PHP versions, about 36,100 were unpatched, including 19,500 running versions that have reached end of life, said Akash Karthi, a security researcher at CloudSEK.You use AI every day. articles.title: Instacart Considers a Potential Sale, Sparking Share Rally
articles.summary: Instacart has explored a potential sale of the grocery-delivery company, a process that has included discussions with Uber Technologies Inc., a person famili...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Instacart has explored a potential sale of the grocery-delivery company, a process that has included discussions with Uber Technologies Inc., a person familiar with the matter said.

Though Instacart recently shopped itself to Uber, the ride-hailing giant walked away from the discussions, according to the person, who asked not to be identified because the talks were private. The two sides are no longer in discussions, the person said.

The Information previously reported that Instacart also held preliminary talks with DoorDash Inc. as part of a potential sale process. The story sent shares of Instacart up as much as 9.2% to $56.44 on Friday.

Representatives for Instacart, which trades as Maplebear Inc., didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Uber and DoorDash also didn't immediately comment in response to requests.

Instacart has been working with an investment bank to evaluate its options, the Information said, citing unidentified people familiar with the matter. Discussions with other companies are early and ongoing and may not result in a deal, according to the report.

The grocery company is exploring a sale at a time of intensifying competition, with Uber and DoorDash encroaching further on its grocery business. That could potentially make a sale to a larger rival the company's best path to delivering returns to shareholders and securing its long-term future.

Uber's stock fell 3.4% in New York trading, while DoorDash declined 3.5%.

articles.body: BERLIN: German companies are exploring investment opportunities in India in precision engineering, aerospace, defence and shipbuilding, besides healthcare, pharmaceuticals and research and development, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said, pointing to growing business interest as European firms look to diversify manufacturing and supply chains.Talking to reporters during his visit to Germany and The Netherlands with a delegation of Indian businesses and startups to explore opportunities in trade, investment and industrial cooperation, Goyal said German companies had publicly announced investments worth $7.4 billion in India with some of these already materialising.More than 2,000 German companies currently operate in India, while cumulative German FDI equity inflows stood at $15.6 billion between April 2000 and March 2026.“With all the regulatory overhang that they (EU) are creating upon themselves, European manufacturing will have to look for trusted partner countries where many of the things that are becoming very expensive in Europe can be produced. articles.summary: Oct 23 (Reuters) - BP announced a deal on Friday that provides Louisiana an accelerated, lump-sum $350 million payment to resolve claims over the 2010 Deepwa...
articles.body:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - BP announced a deal on Friday that provides Louisiana ‌an accelerated, lump-sum $350 million payment to ‌resolve claims over the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill ​and that also settles long-running coastal damage litigation by local parishes.

• BP agreed in 2015 to pay up to $18.7 billion to ‌the federal ⁠government and five states to resolve claims arising out of the oil ⁠spill. That money includes $4.9 billion payable over 18 years to settle economic and other ​claims by ​the states.

• While ​Louisiana had been ‌owed $373 million over the next seven years, the state will now receive a single $350 million payment.

• BP said remaining coastal zone lawsuits by Louisiana parishes will be resolved. ‌It did not provide ​further details.

• "We have now ​disposed of ​claims and settled with all ‌but one of the major ​defendants in ​these coastal cases," Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry, a Republican, said in a ​statement distributed ‌by BP.

articles.title: Upper layer NBFCs have to list: RBI governor on Tatas; dispels doubts on Sept order
articles.summary: Mumbai: In his first public comment since Reserve Bank of India rejected Tata Sons’ bid to shed its non-bank lender status, governor Sanjay Malhotra on
articles.body: Mumbai: In his first public comment since Reserve Bank of India rejected Tata Sons’ bid to shed its non-bank lender status, governor Sanjay Malhotra on Friday left little doubt that the Tata Group holding company must list publicly as long as it remains classified as an upper-layer (UL) non-banking financial company (NBFC) and core investment company (CIC).The remarks appear to settle a debate sparked by Noel Tata, chair of Tata Trusts, Tata Sons’ largest shareholder, who had argued that RBI’s Sept 11 order, which rejected the holding company’s request to deregister as a CIC and directed it to comply with UL-NBFC regulations, did not explicitly mandate a listing.Malhotra’s comments also suggest Tata Sons is in breach of RBI rules. The consequences of continued noncompliance remain unclear.The governor declined to be drawn into the question of Noel Tata’s proposal to merge two Tata Sons subsidiaries with the holding company, a move that could help it sidestep a stock market listing.“NBFCs and CICs, like for example Tata Sons and others, are required to be registered with us because of the systemic risks,” Malhotra said.“As long as it is an NBFC within our definition, it’s a CIC and has access to funds direct or indirect, it’s required to be registered and if it is in the upper layer, it is required to list,” he said at NDTV’s World Summit conference Friday.RBI first classified Tata Sons as an UL-NBFC in 2022 and required it to list within three years. The holding company sought to avoid a market debut by applying to surrender its CIC registration after reducing its debt to zero. But in Sept, the central bank rejected the request, saying it “cannot be acceded to”.‘CICs sit atop group cos, can leverage funds through them’RBI requires UL-NBFCs with assets exceeding Rs 1 lakh crore, or direct or indirect access to public funds, to list. With assets of Rs 2.01 lakh crore as of March 31, 2026, Tata Sons comfortably exceeds the threshold. articles.title: Trump ends tariffs on some Canadian products, aiming to help Senator Collins
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - With an incumbent Maine US senator from his own party locked in a tight reelection battle, President Donald Trump signed an or...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - With an incumbent Maine US senator from his own party locked in a tight reelection battle, President Donald Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could ‌benefit companies from the state.

The Republican president's hefty tariffs on Canada have caused friction with the US neighbor to the north while creating problems for ‌American businesses in Maine and other states that rely on certain Canadian goods.

With the November 3 US midterm elections looming and Republicans fighting to retain control of Congress, Senator Susan Collins had urged the ​White House to address tariffs on products affecting Maine companies and farmers.

Trump's order exempted plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and packing crates and boxes, as well as fresh and dried seaweed, the White House said.

The changes take effect on October 30, four days before the election.

Trump added a number of Canadian products to the 50% tariff list to offset the tariff relief provided in his order, including carpets, paints, shampoos, cocoa powder, wooden coffins, ice cream sticks, air-conditioning machines, chest freezers, archery equipment ‌and canoes.

Collins said the relief will aid Maine's blueberry, potato, ⁠apple and seaweed producers.

"These producers are a vital part of our state's economy and support our rural and coastal communities," Collins said. "Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from ⁠American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense."

Democrat Troy Jackson is seeking to oust Collins in next month's election in a race that polls indicate is very close. The two sparred over tariffs at an October 6 debate.

"Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers," Jackson said on Friday after Trump's action. "Susan Collins enabled this ​chaos, ​voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of ​water to put out the fire."

Trump in August imposed 50% tariffs ‌on $20 billion of Canadian imports, which took effect after talks between the two countries collapsed. Canada retaliated in September with tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on $20 billion in US goods.

Canada and the United States have been engaged in a standoff over the tariffs since Trump imposed them. Trump on Friday asserted that Canada is working on a deal.

Stocks slide as oil prices rise again ahead of midterms

Stocks tumbled on Friday , as oil prices rose again amid the ongoing U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts.

At closing, the Nasdaq Composite was down roughly 53.5 points from Thursday. The index is down by more than 1,600 points since closing time on Oct. 6, when it finished at its highest mark of the year.

The S&P 500, meanwhile, sunk by nearly 40 points since Thursday’s closing. The index dipped as low as 7,612, its lowest point in more than a month.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, is trading at almost $116 per barrel as of Friday, its highest point since late April — roughly two months into the Iran war.

West Texas Intermediate crude, the standard for North American markets, closed at $103.44 , after reaching $103.92 earlier in the day.

The rise in oil prices from geopolitical shocks has carried harsh consequences for Americans, who are paying higher prices at the pump ahead of the midterm elections.

Regular gas costs roughly $4.29 per gallon on average, while the price of a gallon of diesel is above $6.30, according to data from AAA.

That lends President Trump and the GOP a tough hand with voting already underway, as Democrats seek to take control of Congress for the bulk of the president’s final two years in office.

“Gas and diesel prices will continue to skyrocket based on the policies of [Trump] and his Republican enablers,” Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif), the No. 4 House Democrat, wrote Friday on social platform X. “November is coming.”

Oct 23 (Reuters) - Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on Friday that Amazon Web Services' cloud ‌computing capacity is largely sold out through ‌2027, with significant commitments extending into 2028, on growing demand ​for AI infrastructure.

In a video podcast with Andreessen Horowitz co-founder Ben Horowitz and general partner Erik Torenberg, Jassy said Amazon is struggling to keep pace ‌with the insatiable ⁠demand from AI labs and enterprises.

• Earlier this year, Amazon had said it ⁠would spend about $220 billion in capital expenditure for 2026

• Jassy said the company "could invest a lot ​more and ​it wouldn't be ​a bad use of ‌capital," considering cloud-computing capacity for 2026 is already sold out

• "2027 is largely sold out. We always leave a certain amount for on demand and our inference service bedrock, or EC2, but largely ‌sold out all the big ​chunks. A good chunk of ​2028 is sold ​out," he said

• EC2 is an ‌AWS service that provides ​cloud servers for ​running applications, while Bedrock gives customers access to AI models to build generative AI ​applications

• Amazon is ‌scheduled to report third quarter results on ​October 29

articles.title: Quem paga a conta? Economistas analisam promessas de Lula e Flávio diante de Orçamento apertado | G1
articles.standfirst: Com dívida pública de R$ 11,1 trilhões e 90% do Orçamento de 2027 comprometido com despesas obrigatórias, especialistas apontam dificuldades para financiar novas medidas.
articles.summary: Com dívida pública de R$ 11,1 trilhões e 90% do Orçamento de 2027 comprometido com despesas obrigatórias, especialistas apontam dificuldades para financiar novas medidas.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro e Lula chegam ao debate da Globo — Foto: Reprodução

Em uma das eleições mais disputadas da história, os brasileiros vão às urnas neste domingo (25) para escolher o próximo presidente da República entre Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ) e Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ).

Como mostrou o g1 , a principal pauta econômica da eleição é o equilíbrio das contas públicas . As propostas dos presidenciáveis, porém, levantam muitas dúvidas sobre como serão financiadas e quais efeitos terão sobre o Orçamento e a trajetória da dívida pública.

A dívida do país está próxima de R$ 11,1 trilhões . O valor continua crescendo e já equivale a 82,9% do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB). Em outras palavras, o montante corresponde a cerca de 10 meses de tudo o que o país produz em bens e serviços.

O desafio é reverter essa trajetória de alta sem comprometer as políticas públicas. Há bastante tempo, gastos obrigatórios, como os vinculados à Previdência, à saúde e à educação, têm crescido acima do ritmo permitido pelas regras que limitam o aumento das despesas do país.

Evolução da dívida bruta — Foto: — Foto: Arte/g1

Com isso, sobra cada vez menos espaço no Orçamento para investimentos e outros gastos sobre os quais o governo tem maior liberdade para decidir como e quando usar.

Neste mês, o g1 mostrou que, dos R$ 2,8 trilhões previstos em despesas primárias no Orçamento de 2027, 90% estão comprometidos com aposentadorias, salários, benefícios sociais e outras despesas obrigatórias.

Para Murilo Viana, mestre em economia pela Unicamp e especialista em contas públicas, as projeções do Tesouro Nacional já apontam para uma redução dos recursos disponíveis ao governo também nos próximos anos , o que pode limitar ainda mais a capacidade de escolha do próximo presidente sobre onde investir.

O g1 ouviu economistas para avaliar as propostas sobre as contas públicas, os desafios para colocá-las em prática e os riscos para a trajetória da dívida pública. A análise considera não apenas os objetivos anunciados pelos candidatos, mas também os custos das medidas, as fontes de financiamento e os limites do Orçamento.

A Pesquisa de Endividamento e Inadimplência do Consumidor (PEIC), da Confederação Nacional do Comércio de Bens, Serviços e Turismo (CNC), mostra que 81,7% das famílias tinham algum tipo de dívida em setembro. Apesar da leve queda em relação aos 82% registrados em agosto, o endividamento bateu recordes consecutivos ao longo de 2026.

Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro apresentaram propostas para mitigar o problema, mas não detalharam de onde virão os recursos necessários para colocá-las em prática.

Em uma live nas redes sociais e em debates, Flávio propôs que o governo compre dos bancos as dívidas de pessoas e empresas inadimplentes e as renegocie pela Caixa Econômica Federal , com juros menores e prazos mais longos.

O plano prevê um período de carência de seis meses para pessoas físicas e de um ano para empresas, durante o qual os devedores não precisariam pagar as parcelas .

Outra proposta é o programa “Ganha-Ganha”, que prevê a concessão de pontos para quem mantiver as contas em dia ou fizer cursos de capacitação. Esses pontos poderiam ser trocados por benefícios, como juros menores e cashback.

“Utilizar a Caixa Econômica Federal para fazer esse tipo de operação é um risco gigantesco de transferir a dívida privada para uma instituição pública”, afirma Murilo Viana, mestre em economia pela Unicamp e especialista em finanças públicas.

Daniel Duque, economista do Instituto Brasileiro de Economia da Fundação Getulio Vargas ( FGV Ibre), também alerta para possíveis impactos na oferta de crédito. Segundo ele, a expectativa de novas renegociações pode mudar o comportamento de bancos e consumidores.

“Isso vai ter consequências sobre as análises de crédito futuras. Os bancos podem pensar: se o governo pode fazer isso agora, quem garante que não fará de novo daqui a dois anos?”, diz Duque.

Já o presidente Lula, candidato à reeleição, anunciou uma série de medidas já durante a campanha eleitoral. Na última quarta-feira (21), sancionou uma lei que perdoa dívidas de microempreendedores individuais (MEIs) com a União.

A medida abrange dívidas de impostos e contribuições federais, incluindo contribuições previdenciárias em atraso, além de multas, juros e encargos de cobrança. Segundo o governo, mais de 3,6 milhões de empreendedores poderão ser beneficiados.

O governo também incluiu os MEIs no Desenrola 3.0, programa voltado à renegociação de dívidas bancárias. A iniciativa prevê que o governo compre dos bancos conjuntos de dívidas de clientes, conhecidos como carteiras de crédito. As instituições financeiras terão de oferecer descontos de pelo menos 90%. O valor total dessas dívidas foi estimado em cerca de R$ 6 bilhões .

As medidas também levantam dúvidas sobre seus efeitos nas contas públicas. Isso porque o perdão de dívidas elimina valores que a União tinha a receber, enquanto a compra de dívidas bancárias exige o uso de recursos públicos.

“Pessoas e bancos acabam esperando para agir: ‘o governo vai fazer essa renegociação, então não vou pagar porque vai sair mais barato eu esperar pelo próximo programa’”, afirma Daniel Duque, que também menciona as duas edições anteriores do Desenrola.

Cortes de gastos ou aumento das receitas?

Integrante da equipe econômica de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), Daniella Marques (Republicanos) afirmou no início do mês que o plano do candidato à Presidência prevê cortar gastos equivalentes a 1,5% do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) , revisar o arcabouço fiscal e reduzir a estrutura do governo.

A campanha chama o conjunto de medidas de "tesouraço" , mas a campanha nunca detalhou quais gastos seriam cortados, em quanto tempo e como os cortes seriam feitos.

O economista Ricardo Hammoud, do FGV Ibre, avalia que promessas genéricas de melhorar a eficiência do governo não são suficientes para reduzir significativamente os gastos públicos. Segundo ele, é difícil fazer cortes mais profundos porque grande parte do Orçamento já está comprometida com despesas obrigatórias.

“Flávio prometeu melhorar a eficiência do gasto público, mas isso ainda é muito pontual. Para fazer mudanças estruturais, são necessárias reformas que permitam alterar regras de despesas obrigatórias”, afirma Hammoud.

As despesas obrigatórias — como aposentadorias e pensões do INSS, benefícios do Bolsa Família, salários de servidores e o Benefício de Prestação Continuada (BPC) — seguem regras previstas em lei. Por isso, o governo tem menos liberdade para reduzir esses gastos de uma hora para outra. Cortes mais profundos podem exigir mudanças nas leis ou na Constituição.

“Medidas de ajuste são impopulares no curto prazo. É fácil defender um ajuste fiscal, mas, quando é preciso apontar onde cortar, a decisão acaba afetando diretamente diferentes políticas públicas”, diz Murilo Viana.

O presidente Lula, por sua vez, prevê ampliar os gastos com programas como o Pé-de-Meia e o Bolsa Família , manter o programa de valorização do salário mínimo e aumentar os investimentos públicos.

Essas medidas podem ajudar a sustentar a renda das famílias e financiar serviços e obras, mas também pressionam o Orçamento quando não há receitas suficientes para bancá-las.

Hammoud, da FGV, questiona a estratégia de aumentar os gastos públicos contando com uma arrecadação maior para compensá-los. Para ele, o ajuste das contas públicas deveria priorizar o controle das despesas.

“O arcabouço fiscal fracassou no controle da dívida. Em 2023, o governo prometeu conter o aumento dos gastos e estabilizar a dívida, mas não entregou o resultado esperado”, afirma.

Flávio Bolsonaro também promete rever pontos da reforma tributária em curso , reduzir impostos e encargos e retomar um programa que concedia benefícios tributários a empresas do setor de eventos.

🔍 O Programa Emergencial de Retomada do Setor de Eventos (Perse) oferecia benefícios tributários, incluindo alíquotas zero de alguns impostos federais. O programa foi encerrado em 2025 pelo governo Lula, que justificou a decisão pelo alto custo para os cofres públicos e apontou indícios de irregularidades no uso dos benefícios por algumas empresas. Na ocasião, o ministro da Fazenda, Fernando Haddad, afirmou que o governo poderia deixar de arrecadar cerca de R$ 20 bilhões em 2025 caso o programa fosse mantido.

"O maior programa de incentivos aos artistas e eventos foi criado em 2021. Sabem quem fez: o Jair. Vou restabelecer o Perse para todo setor de eventos culturais, shows, turismo, que hoje estão sufocados, endividados pela crise que esse governo colocou o país inteiro", declarou o candidato do PL nas redes sociais.

Além do Perse, Daniella Marques afirmou que um eventual governo do PL pretende acabar com o chamado "split payment", mecanismo previsto na reforma tributária que separa automaticamente o valor do imposto no momento do pagamento de uma compra. O objetivo é reduzir a sonegação fiscal.

O tributarista Lucas Ribeiro, fundador e CEO da ROIT, empresa de tecnologia voltada a soluções para a reforma tributária, estimou no ano passado que o "split payment" poderia aumentar a arrecadação federal em R$ 400 bilhões a R$ 500 bilhões por ano — montante que, segundo ele, equivale ao valor dos impostos sonegados.

Para Ricardo Hammoud, a situação das contas públicas deixa pouco espaço para reduzir impostos ou abrir mão de arrecadação. Embora considere elevada a carga tributária brasileira, ele afirma que a prioridade deve ser o controle da dívida pública.

“Sou favorável à redução de impostos e considero a carga tributária brasileira muito alta em comparação com a de outros países emergentes. Mas não há espaço hoje para cortar tributos. A prioridade precisa ser a dívida pública. Se Flávio fizer isso inicialmente, poderá gerar dúvidas sobre a responsabilidade fiscal que tanto defende”, afirma.

Já o presidente Lula sancionou nesta semana uma lei que perdoa dívidas de microempreendedores individuais (MEIs). Segundo o governo, a medida prevê o perdão integral de R$ 12,6 bilhões em dívidas de cerca de 3,6 milhões de MEIs.

A medida abrange dívidas com a União inscritas na Dívida Ativa até 13 de outubro de 2026, referentes às contribuições dos microempreendedores, incluindo juros, multas e encargos legais.

Também foi estabelecido um aumento gradual do limite de faturamento anual dos MEIs para R$ 140 mil até 2028, o que permitirá que esses empreendedores aumentem suas receitas sem precisar sair do regime simplificado.

A economista Juliana Inhasz, professora do Insper, avalia que propostas voltadas aos microempreendedores também têm apelo eleitoral, especialmente entre trabalhadores por conta própria e pequenos empresários.

Para ela, porém, as promessas de benefícios sempre precisam explicar de onde virão os recursos para financiá-los.

“Há propostas que não se sustentam quando se pergunta de onde virá o dinheiro. Sem uma fonte de financiamento definida, fica difícil saber como seriam executadas”, afirma Inhasz.

Entre as propostas, há medidas de injeção direta de recursos públicos na economia. Flávio propõe o ViraPIX , que prevê a devolução de parte dos valores pagos pela população em despesas como contas de luz, prestações e taxas, por meio do PIX.

O programa poderia aumentar a renda disponível das famílias e estimular o consumo, mas a campanha ainda não detalhou quem teria direito ao benefício, quais seriam os valores e como a iniciativa seria financiada.

A ideia também é muito semelhante ao cashback, já definido pela reforma tributária, que devolve parte do imposto para população de baixa renda inscrita no Cadastro Único (CadÚnico).

Lula, por sua vez, propõe ampliar o Bolsa Família e oferecer transporte público gratuito aos fins de semana , além de manter os subsídios aos combustíveis.

No caso do Bolsa Família, a ampliação do número de beneficiários ou do valor pago por família aumenta os gastos permanentes do governo com o programa.

Já a tarifa zero aos fins de semana dependeria da definição de como o benefício seria financiado e de como os custos seriam divididos entre União, estados e municípios.

Os subsídios aos combustíveis, por sua vez, podem aumentar os gastos públicos quando pagos diretamente pelo governo ou reduzir a arrecadação quando concedidos por meio de isenções ou reduções de impostos.

Para Ricardo Hammoud, economista do FGV Ibre, o peso das despesas obrigatórias no Orçamento reduz o espaço disponível para investimentos e outros gastos sobre os quais o governo tem maior liberdade de decisão.

Assim, seria necessário cortar gastos em outras áreas para abrir espaço para novos programas ou para a ampliação dos já existentes.

articles.title: INSS: faltou ao 1º turno? Votar no segundo pode servir como prova de vida; veja como funciona | G1
articles.standfirst: Beneficiários podem comprovar que estão vivos automaticamente ao votar em 25 de outubro, mesmo que tenham faltado à primeira votação; ausência nas urnas não bloqueia o pagamento do INSS.
articles.summary: Beneficiários podem comprovar que estão vivos automaticamente ao votar em 25 de outubro, mesmo que tenham faltado à primeira votação.
articles.body:
Ir às urnas no segundo turno das eleições , no domingo (25), pode servir como prova de vida para aposentados, pensionistas e beneficiários de programas assistenciais do Instituto Nacional do Seguro Social (INSS).

A comprovação é feita automaticamente, por meio do cruzamento de dados entre a Justiça Eleitoral e a Previdência Social. Não é necessário apresentar documentos nem ir a uma agência.

Quem não votou no primeiro turno também pode usar a votação do segundo para comprovar que está vivo. A ausência na primeira votação não invalida o comparecimento à segunda.

Segundo o INSS, a integração dos sistemas com a Justiça Eleitoral já está em funcionamento.

Em 2024, a participação nas eleições contribuiu para atualizar a prova de vida de aproximadamente 5 milhões de pessoas.

Como funciona a prova de vida pelo voto?

A prova de vida é um procedimento usado pelo INSS para confirmar que o beneficiário está vivo e manter os pagamentos regulares. A comprovação pode ser feita de diferentes formas, entre elas o comparecimento às urnas.

Quando o eleitor vota, a Justiça Eleitoral registra a informação, que pode ser cruzada com os dados da Previdência Social. O processo ocorre automaticamente . O beneficiário não precisa guardar o comprovante de votação nem solicitar a atualização.

Tenho 70 anos ou mais: sou obrigado a votar?

As regras eleitorais não devem ser confundidas com as da prova de vida do INSS . Pessoas com 70 anos ou mais não são obrigadas a votar e, por isso, não precisam justificar a ausência.

Quem é obrigado a votar precisa regularizar a ausência no primeiro turno, mesmo que compareça ao segundo. Nesse caso, o voto no segundo turno pode valer como prova de vida, mas não substitui a regularização da falta na primeira votação.

➡️ A justificativa eleitoral não vale como prova de vida. Para que a participação na eleição seja considerada pelo INSS, é necessário comparecer às urnas.

Não . Segundo o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), a ausência às urnas não provoca o bloqueio automático do benefício do INSS .

Quem não votar pode fazer a prova de vida por outros meios aceitos pelo instituto . Para verificar a situação, o beneficiário pode acessar o aplicativo ou o site Meu INSS e selecionar a opção "Prova de Vida".

Também é possível consultar informações pela Central 135.

articles.title: From fuel price hikes to cost-of-living concerns, US consumer sentiment nears record low
articles.summary: US consumer sentiment edged down to near a record low in October as rising prices linked to the Middle East conflict weighed on households' views of the
articles.body: US consumer sentiment edged down to near a record low in October as rising prices linked to the Middle East conflict weighed on households' views of the economy, a University of Michigan survey showed on Friday, with affordability emerging as a key issue ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.The university's Consumer Sentiment Index slipped to 48.0 this month from a final reading of 48.1 in September.Economists polled by Reuters had expected a reading of 46.3, which was also the preliminary estimate for October.October's reading was the second-lowest on record, following the all-time low of 44.8 recorded in May, shortly after the Iran war began."Purchasing power continues to dominate consumer views of the economy," said Joanne Hsu, director of the Surveys of Consumers. "Sentiment is now 10% below a year ago and 15% less than February, just prior to the Iran conflict."Independent voters report weaker sentimentThe survey's findings coincided with political polling showing that voters held a dim view of the economy and President Donald Trump's and the Republican Party's handling of it, Reuters reported.Millions of Americans have already cast early ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress for the final two years of Trump's term.Polls indicated Republicans were likely to lose control of the House of Representatives, with the Senate also potentially at stake. Trump's approval rating in a Reuters/Ipsos poll stood at a record low, amid a surge in fuel prices following his decision to attack Iran in late February.The University of Michigan survey found that the decline in sentiment was driven by respondents who identified as independents, a group that includes swing voters.Their sentiment score fell to 42.4 in October from 47.7 in September, putting it just above May's record low of 40.6. Sentiment scores among Democrats and Republicans improved.The survey also found that more independents and Republicans were citing high prices as a strain on their personal finances. Since January, the number of independents reporting inflation pressures as a financial burden had risen by 27%, while the figure among Republicans had increased by 52%. Among Democrats, the increase was 15%.Households with little or no exposure to the stock market had also increasingly cited high prices as a financial burden compared with the beginning of the year. The stock market had recently climbed rapidly amid enthusiasm for investments in artificial intelligence.Inflation expectations remain elevatedThe survey's measure of consumers' expectations for inflation over the next 12 months rose to 4.7% in October from 4.6% in September. The measure had stood at 3.4% in February, before the US-Israeli war with Iran began.Expectations for inflation over the next five years increased to 3.5% from 3.4% in September and 3.2% in March, shortly after the conflict began.In an accompanying report, Hsu said persistently elevated inflation expectations in the period following the Covid-19 pandemic posed a risk to the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring inflation down to its 2% target. The target had remained unmet for more than five years, she wrote."Consumers broadly expect inflation to accelerate, and this year’s increases in inflation expectations are not limited to one part of the political spectrum," Hsu said.She also cautioned that relatively resilient consumer spending, despite negative views of the economy, required close attention. If households were spending now to avoid expected price increases in the future, bringing inflation down could become more difficult, she added.Federal Reserve decision due next weekFederal Reserve officials are scheduled to meet in Washington next week. Despite recent inflation readings that came in higher than expected, they were broadly expected to keep the policy interest rate unchanged at 3.75%-4.00%.The Fed had raised the rate by a quarter of a percentage point in September. Most officials had indicated a need for higher interest rates, while key policymakers had also expressed willingness to wait for more data before making their next move.You use AI every day. articles.title: India needs to scale up battery storage alongside renewable energy: Experts
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India needs to expand battery storage and grid infrastructure alongside renewable energy capacity to ensure reliable power supply as it moves
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India needs to expand battery storage and grid infrastructure alongside renewable energy capacity to ensure reliable power supply as it moves towards its target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030, experts said at an industry event.The country has crossed 300 GW of installed non-fossil fuel capacity, but integrating more renewable power into the grid will require investment in energy storage, domestic manufacturing and research, said Jai Asundi, executive director of the Centre for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP).The discussions took place at the Renewable Energy India Expo, held alongside The Battery Show India and the Energy Storage Summit India in Greater Noida.Yogesh Mudras, managing director of Informa Markets in India, said renewable energy generation and grid storage must expand together as India’s clean energy market grows. “We have reached an execution phase where generation and grid storage must scale in tandem,” he said, adding that India’s renewable energy market was projected to reach 486 GW by 2030, while its battery storage sector was expected to cross $8.5 billion by 2031.Anandi Iyer, director of the Fraunhofer Office in India, said the world added around 800 GW of renewable energy capacity in 2025, while global battery storage deployment reached 108 GW, up 40% from the previous year. She said India and Germany could work together in battery research, power electronics and advanced engineering.Australia’s high commissioner to India, Philip Green, said the two countries could combine Australia’s critical mineral resources and solar technology with India’s manufacturing capabilities to strengthen clean energy supply chains. Australia produces more than half of the world’s lithium, he said.Scotland First Minister John Swinney said Scottish expertise and innovation could complement India’s manufacturing scale and market potential to support the clean energy transition.Manu Srivastav, additional chief secretary in Madhya Pradesh’s power and renewable energy department, said falling technology costs and economies of scale were making renewable energy increasingly competitive with conventional power.The three-day event, which opened on Thursday, has over 1,080 exhibitors and 1,400 brands, with participation from more than 10 countries.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'German companies no longer see India only as a market, but as their partner': Piyush Goyal
articles.summary: German companies are increasingly looking at India as a strategic base for manufacturing, research and development (R&D), and innovation, in addition to
articles.body: German companies are increasingly looking at India as a strategic base for manufacturing, research and development (R&D), and innovation, in addition to viewing it as an important consumer market, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal has said.Speaking to the media after completing his two-day visit, Goyal said he held several bilateral meetings with representatives of major German companies, including Siemens healthcare, Bertelsmann investment, Volkswagen and Skoda.“The CEOs echoed one message — German companies no longer see India only as a market, but as their partner, as a base for manufacturing, for research and development, for innovation,” he said.Goyal said the combination of German precision and research capabilities with India's skilled workforce, talent and manufacturing potential could reshape global perceptions of the country. He also highlighted the opportunities arising from investments in India's growth story.Around 2,000 German companies currently operate in India. The minister's visit focused on exploring ways to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries, according to the news agency PTI.He said the bilateral relationship could facilitate not only trade in goods and services but also greater collaboration in talent development, innovation, co-creation, co-design, co-development and joint manufacturing.“The focus of this visit has been to translate this partnership to greater levels of investment, industrial cooperation, and research and development,” Goyal said.He added that the success of the India-European union free trade agreement (FTA) in the coming years would be reflected in increased business activity, new orders, higher investments and technology partnerships.Negotiations for the India-EU trade agreement were concluded in January. The pact is expected to be signed by the end of this year and could come into effect next year.German companies plan to expand India operationsGoyal said German businesses were increasingly considering India as a manufacturing destination as they seek to lower costs and improve their competitiveness in international markets.“Today the greatest imperative before German industry is to cut costs and become more competitive in global markets. Therefore, they are looking at manufacturing in a much greater degree in India,” he said.He noted that German companies were also expanding their innovation and design activities in the country through existing centres and global capability centres (GCCs), which employ large numbers of skilled Indian professionals.According to Goyal, India has more than 2,100 GCCs employing millions of people. Their workforce ranges from a few hundred employees at smaller facilities to several lakh at larger centres.He said German companies were preparing for substantial expansions in India, with most planning to double or triple their operations over the next two to five years.Describing the level of interest among German businesses as significant, Goyal said deeper engagement could eventually lead to more joint innovation and product development.He also invited German research institutions to establish a stronger presence in India and take the partnership forward through greater scientific and technological cooperation.India-EU FTA and CBAMGoyal said the European union recognised India's efforts to tackle climate change and its progress in meeting commitments under the Paris agreement, including achieving its intended nationally determined contributions ahead of schedule.He added that European countries were interested in collaborating with India on green hydrogen, financial assistance and other green initiatives.Addressing his comments on the EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) at the Berlin global dialogue a day earlier, Goyal maintained that his remarks were based on facts. He also acknowledged that Europe had made considerable progress on environmental issues and said cooperation between Europe and India in this area was advancing rapidly.The minister had warned that the EU risked inviting “disaster” through the imposition of CBAM, questioning the historical responsibility of developed countries for climate change.“Who's responsible for this (climate change) mess in the first place? Where did this ozone layer get damaged? Who sent all that carbon up there?” he had asked during the discussion.When another panellist responded that all countries shared responsibility, Goyal disagreed, pointing out that India accounts for around 17% of the world's population but contributes less than 3% of global carbon emissions.Referring to the 2015 Paris agreement, he argued that developed countries, having benefited from decades of industrial growth, had agreed to bear a greater share of the burden and provide support to developing and less-developed nations.“Eleven years later, we haven't seen a nickel or a dime of that. It's all promises,” he said.Goyal also argued that European countries had contributed significantly to the climate crisis while relying on coal to maintain low energy costs during their industrial expansion.He stressed that India, meanwhile, was pursuing one of the world's fastest-growing clean energy programmes.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump’s $8 billion farm lifeline won’t fully solve farmers’ diesel problem
articles.summary: The Trump administration’s $8 billion relief program for farmers is throwing a lifeline to the industry, but producers are still facing lower margins due to high diesel prices amid the Iran war — and experts say the move might only buy time for solving deeper challenges. Through the initiative announced earlier this week, farmers will…
articles.body:
The Trump administration’s $8 billion relief program for farmers is throwing a lifeline to the industry, but producers are still facing lower margins due to high diesel prices amid the Iran war — and experts say the move might only buy time for solving deeper challenges.

Through the initiative announced earlier this week, farmers will receive “one-time” payments from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) in the midst of harvest season.

But diesel remains above $6 per gallon on average, and President Trump has not indicated he will wind down the nearly eight-month Iran conflict in the near future, even as Republicans in the farm-heavy heartland face national economic headwinds ahead of the midterms.

A gallon of diesel costs roughly $6.32 on average in the U.S., according to data from AAA . That is down about 20 cents from a month ago but still nearly $2.80 greater than a year ago.

And it could take up to two years for the diesel market to return to normal, with the clock only starting when the Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars end, says Max Pyziur, the director of downstream, transportation fuels and natural gas projects at the Energy Policy Research Foundation.

“I think it’s going to take a long time,” he said.

Diesel price spikes , in tandem with elevated fertilizer costs , dealt farmers a difficult hand during the spring planting season. The $8 billion program will help — especially going into 2027, says Dr. Faith Parum, the deputy chief economist at the American Farm Bureau Federation.

“It will help our farmers make … the math make a little bit more sense as they sit down towards the end of the year and think about what’s next, and what’s 2027 look like,” Parum told The Hill.

“This is really helpful as they sit down with lenders, extension agents, and all of those trusted folks to think about what their farm looks like in 2027,” she added.

Parum noted the agricultural economy, much like the rest of the country, is “very diesel intensive,” with high fuel prices posing a challenge to corn, soybean, wheat and other row crop farmers.

“All of your row crop guys have been in a consecutive downturn for the last four years. In fact, most folks … [are] losing money per acre,” she said, noting increased diesel costs “are just putting more pressure” on farmers.

Much of the machinery that farmers use, from tractors to combines, runs on diesel. Tractor sales were down by 16.4 percent year-over-year in September, according to data from the Association of Equipment Manufacturers.

Trains that carry grain across the country also rely on the refined fuel, as Scott Irwin, the chair of agricultural marketing at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, noted Friday.

“It’s not an understatement to say that the crop sector runs on diesel. Without diesel, food production would ultimately stop,” Irwin told The Hill.

The USDA will calculate the amount of support farmers receive from the $8 billion pot through a formula that combines self-reported acreage data to the department’s Farm Service Agency (FSA), cost of production estimates from its Economic Research Service and yields and pricing data from its monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates manual .

The FSA will release payment rates for “Title I” commodities, which include barley, corn, long- and short-grain rice, soybeans and wheat, in November.

A spokesperson for the USDA said the relief program is an “additional source of relief for years of elevated input costs, diminished export markets, and lackluster domestic agriculture policy.”

The administration earlier this year provided hundreds of thousands of farmers impacted by Trump’s tariffs a combined $12 billion in payments.

That relief was meant to be a bridge to nearly $14 billion in total risk and price loss coverage payments it sent this month under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in July 2025.

“The Harvest Fuel Relief Program is a short-term solution that will allow for long term success,” the USDA spokesperson added.

Trump touted the program on Monday during a campaign stop in Kansas, saying that GOP Sen. Roger Marshall (Kan.) “got it to happen.”

Marshall is facing a tough reelection battle against Democrat Adam Hamilton in Kansas, a heavy agricultural state.

Parum said farmers are “thankful” for the administration’s latest relief, while Irwin said it will be “quite helpful” for corn and soybean farmers. But looking ahead, diesel prices still project to strain producers’ bottom lines for the foreseeable future.

Pyziur, of the Energy Policy Research Foundation, said the Iran and Ukraine wars have resulted in a global shortage of about 1.5 to 1.6 million barrels of diesel per day. He attributed 70 percent of the diminished capacity to the Middle Eastern conflict and 30 percent to the eastern European war.

“It’s not the fact that you’re impairing transit or movements. It’s also the fact that you’ve damaged an awful lot of refining capacity,” he said, referencing Iranian strikes on refineries in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Ukrainian attacks on Russian facilities.

Even before this year’s rise in diesel prices, agricultural producers were in a pinch, with the USDA estimating in September that farm debt would hit a record $605.1 billion this year.

The amount of farms that filed for Chapter 12 bankruptcies increased by 46 percent from 2024 to 2025, according to data from the Farm Bureau.

Irwin referenced Trump’s trade war with China, which reduced soybean exports last year, as a source of “uncertainty” for the industry. Inflation has also run above the Federal Reserve’s target of 2 percent for five and a half years, increasing this year during the Iran conflict.

“Farmers are paying much higher insurance costs … benefit costs, repair costs for all the machinery, all that’s gone up,” he added.

Parum also cited an “erosion of working capital” for why the economic landscape is squeezing farmers.

That erosion has caused many farmers to endure four to five straight years of “tight to negative” margins, she noted.

“They may have used a lot of their cash reserves and working capital to make it through previous years. And so that’s really where we’re starting to see that debt level become more worrisome,” Parum said.

“Ad hoc assistance is helpful, but we’re really looking for ways … [to] fix this structural issue,” she added.

articles.title: Apple's new hardware push is meeting AI-worried investors at the right moment
articles.summary: Apple offers a hardware refuge during a moment of AI volatility.
articles.body:
Armed with a brand new hardware lineup, Apple ( AAPL ) has launched a campaign to reclaim the top spot as the most valuable company on the stock market, briefly succeeding on Friday.

The hardware push, led by new CEO John Ternus, is an ambitious shift from his predecessor Tim Cook's services-first strategy. And, coincidentally, it's timed for maximum investor appreciation, happening just as the AI trade is losing steam and fresh fears over AI financing and a slowdown in capital spending have rattled investors.

A new hardware lineup comes as a refuge during a moment of volatility. And Apple's cash pile and earning machine, protected from enormous compute commitments and shifting AI sentiment, is an attractive alternative. The new iPhone Duo is anything but vaporware.

This week, several of Apple's tech peers have drawn investor attention for the wrong reasons. Most notably, Meta ( META ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) rekindled concerns over AI financing. Though both companies undershot expectations for AI spending for the short-term, any sense of financial discipline was lost as investors grasped the magnitude of their future plans.

Longer-term, off-balance-sheet spending plans of $825 billion for Meta and a $100 billion chip plant estimate for Tesla showed that bigger capex bills will be due in the near future. Other factors swirling around the AI world amplified the selling pressure. AI valuations are under scrutiny as SK Hynix became the latest tech firm to pause a spin-off IPO; the cost of tokens is falling as more users rely on open-weight and less sophisticated models; and global credit markets are flashing risk-off signals . All of this was enough to push the 10-year Treasury yield back under 5%.

Cupertino wrestling once again with AI darling Nvidia is a testament to the iPhone-maker's strategy and a punctuation mark to all that AI drama. It also isn't the first time Apple has seized the moment to capitalize on shifting AI sentiment.

At the height of AI doomer panic last month, Apple flooded tech and business media with the feel-good launch of a new iPhone. The presentation had the company's signature look, calm and full of white space, a sharp contrast with the AI anxiety swirling just outside its glass doors.

The message from the keynote was simple: Apple wants to sell you its most capable iPhone yet, with a few nifty AI tools built in. AI was some finishing salt, though. The glossy hardware was the meal.

While rival tech companies and AI labs were busy stoking fears of Terminator-style catastrophe and mass job losses, Apple was having an entirely different conversation. Now, amid fresh investor jitters over AI spending, Apple looks to have zagged against its peers once again. The iPhone Duo came out on Friday. It's pushing into new hardware territory , broadening its lineup and giving people more reasons to enter, and stay inside, its seamless ecosystem.

articles.title: How do you help a spouse who’s buried in debt? An expert weighs in
articles.summary: The source of your spouse’s debt problems should inform how you both approach the issue.
articles.body: If your partner is in a tough spot financially and you want to help cure the problem, you might take a beat to consider the circumstance holistically before doing anything. In this week’s Ask the Expert for CNN’s Savings Challenge, Douglas Boneparth, certified financial planner and founder of Bone Fide Wealth, offers one reader advice on the best way to approach the issue of his wife’s large debts. The reader wrote: “Hi Doug, my wife has $20k in credit card debt and $100k+ in student loans. She’s not the best at managing her money and I want to help her with a plan to manage her debt. How can I help?” DOUG: First, let me just say that the fact that you want to help her says a lot about you. But let me reframe this just a bit because I think it is going to matter. You said she’s “not the best at managing her money.” Before doing anything, I’d encourage you to get curious about why she ran up so much debt. Does she have anxiety around money? Was she never taught how to manage it? Or did she run up credit card debt because her income wasn’t enough to cover her basic living costs? The answer changes everything about how you help her. For instance, if she racked up debt to pay for essential expenses over time, no debt payoff strategy will work until the income side gets addressed too. But if that’s not the issue, here’s how I’d suggest you and she approach the debt itself. The credit card debt is the most urgent. Those rates are likely somewhere between 20% and 29%, which is brutal. That gets attacked first, aggressively. For the student loans, you need to know the interest rates before deciding how hard to push. Federal loans may have income-driven repayment options or even forgiveness pathways depending on her profession, so don’t just throw money at them before understanding what you’re working with. For a practical starting point, try the avalanche method. That’s when you pay minimums on everything, then throw every extra dollar at the highest-rate debt, so it gets paid off first. It’s mathematically optimal. Some people, however, prefer the snowball method (smallest balance first) because the psychological wins keep them motivated. Both work. I like avalanche but she should pick the one she’ll stick with. Tip of the week: Pay yourself first Make savings happen automatically so you don’t have to think about it. Even small amounts add up over time. Decide how much of your paycheck you want to go into a high-yield savings account (you’ll find the best yields offered by online banks). Then tell your employer to direct deposit that amount from every paycheck into your savings account. It’s the same pay-yourself-first principle as when your employer automatically transfers a percentage of your pay into your workplace retirement plan.

articles.title: Couple weighed down by debt gets a small inheritance. An expert gives advice on how to manage it
articles.summary: Mariza and Geffrey Gordon used a modest inheritance to help to pay down their debt. But they still need to reevaluate how they manage their money.
articles.body: The last time CNN checked in with Mariza and Geffrey Gordon, the Milwaukee-based couple weighed down by debt who hoped to build an emergency fund and stop living paycheck to paycheck, they’d just gotten disappointing news. They’d been told because of their credit scores, they didn’t qualify for a balance transfer card, which would have given them up to 21 months to pay off their nearly $40,000 in credit card debt interest free. Nor did they qualify for a personal loan at a lower rate to pay off what they owe. And the terms they were offered on a debt management plan just weren’t feasible for them. A month later, though, the couple’s circumstances had changed: They received a modest inheritance from a relative – a big chunk of which they used to pay off their credit card debts. That freed up the roughly $1,400 a month they had been spending to make their minimum required payments. While that has been a huge weight off their shoulders, it didn’t erase their need to rethink how they manage money so that they no longer just get by. Nor did it erase the fact that Mariza’s two months of severance from her former job were about to run out. With her upcoming unemployment benefits, their monthly household income would be about $2,000 lower than it was when she was working. Plus, she still had to arrange for health insurance coverage, since they’d missed a deadline to add her to her husband’s employer plan. Zero credit card debt is great, but … When the couple shared news of their inheritance with Tiffany Aliche, the financial educator they’ve been working with, she advised them to come up with a plan before doing anything. But they emailed her soon after to say they used a large piece of it to clear their credit card debts. While that wasn’t a bad decision, Tiffany said, she would have preferred they’d first taken a beat to consider how much money to set aside to cover them until Mariza finds a new job. Tiffany said she might have suggested only paying off half their credit card debt, thereby improving their credit scores enough to qualify for a 0% interest balance transfer card, and then letting the rest of their money earn 4% in an online high-yield savings account until their financial circumstances stabilize. Nevertheless, Tiffany said, “They were excited about doing the responsible thing. They did what they thought was right.” But now she wants to work with them to interrupt their money patterns and have them think more holistically about their full financial picture. “I’m trying to reframe for them. Let’s disrupt your pattern and come up with a new [one] that can work for you,” she said. The good news … While the couple left Tiffany with the impression that they’d already spent some of their remaining inheritance to help both Mariza’s sons buy cars and to make some home improvements, in fact, they’d only given one son $5,000 already. They put the remainder of their inheritance in a high-yield savings account, they told CNN. And, Geffrey added, he is going to aim to save 20% of his paycheck every month. He said he already set up direct deposits into two new high-yield savings accounts, one of which had a 4% annual percentage yield. What’s next: We’ll follow up with Mariza and Geffrey in a few weeks. But next week, Jeff Kizer learns about the debt pay-down strategy that may get him to a comfortable retirement at age 75.

articles.title: Winter is coming. For Maine families, it’s never been more expensive.
articles.summary: The soaring cost of energy and heating oil is one reason why the economy remains a top issue for Maine voters. Even more so in Aroostook County, where 16% of all residents and 12% of seniors live in poverty.
articles.body: Behind the steering wheel of his silver pickup, Scott Bates fills in the blanks with numbers. It’s 8:51 a.m., and at $4.85 a gallon, heating oil is 11 cents cheaper than the night before. He could buy 1,000 gallons and sell each for around $5.25. But not $5.55, because this is a crisis. What if he didn’t get paid for any of the day’s deliveries? Some quick math in his head confirmed that his company, Bates Fuel, would be on the hook for $48,000, and it isn’t even winter yet. “We need dollar drops,” he said, refreshing an app on his phone that tracks minute-by-minute oil prices. “We’re getting cent drops.” This is Bates’ front-row seat to Maine’s unique economic hardship. Here, around 50% of homes rely on fuel oil as their main heat source, more than any other state. The soaring cost of energy and heating oil is one reason why the economy remains a top issue for Maine voters, just days before the midterm elections. Even more so in Bates’ home of Aroostook County, which swallows some 6,700 square miles way up near the Canadian border. In the largest county east of the Mississippi, the closest grocery store can easily be an hour away. Politicians and pundits call it “affordability.” In Aroostook, that’s an empty kerosene tank, kids sleeping in snowsuits and parents lining their windows with plastic sheets to keep the draft from crawling in. Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson, the late-breaking Democratic candidate, are neck-and-neck, trying to convince Mainers that they have the answers. Collins this month announced the early release of $38 million in federal home heating assistance after working with Trump officials. She has worked with the administration to insulate Maine industries from the trade war, including some tariff relief announced on Friday. And she successfully pressed the administration to release more home heating oil that had been in reserve. Jackson has talked about growing up fearful his family would run out of heat. He says the ultimate answer to today’s crisis is to end the war in Iran. His campaign directs voters to resources like wood banks and programs for overdue bills. Both candidates know Aroostook’s challenges. Collins is a self-described “County girl” from Caribou. Jackson is a fifth-generation logger from Allagash. This week, Maine’s Department of Energy Resources said that residents statewide would pay around $750 more than last year to fill a standard 275-gallon tank to capacity. Heating oil costs had just hit a record high of $6.04 per gallon, an 83% increase from this time last year. That’s $750 many in Aroostook County simply don’t have. Families could easily refill their tanks four or five times from now until spring. And prices won’t necessarily plunge if the Iran war ends. Bates has been letting so many customers slide that he hasn’t turned a profit since April. “This is the first time in 36 years I have felt like enough’s enough,” Bates, 69, said. “This is too much for everybody.” Bates pulls over and checks his phone. It’s 10 a.m., and heating oil is up 6 cents, to $4.91 a gallon. He could wait and hope for a tick down. Or the price could edge past $5, and he’d regret it all night. He buys 1,000 gallons. An order confirmation pops up – an animated green checkmark decorated with rainbow confetti. ‘This is the United States’ In early October, the trees in Aroostook County are blanketed in fiery reds, oranges and yellows. Already, a third of Bates’ customers are running on credit. His drivers are setting out for more “50s,” shorthand for the households that can only afford 50 gallons at a time. There’s usually a service charge for such small deliveries. After all, it’s costing a lot more lately to fuel a delivery truck. But Bates waived the fee this season. The morning fog had lifted as Bates trails one of his delivery trucks and its driver, Lee Wood. Beyond the foliage and some grazing cows was a clear view of Mount Katahdin, Maine’s highest peak. He points out a power plant that employed locals for decades, then shuttered as the biomass industry struggled. Founded in 1989, Bates Fuel had made it through the Great Recession and the pandemic. But the math is getting harder. Benchmark prices on the global oil market are set by traders “sitting back in some corporate office somewhere,” Bates said. Wood pulls the delivery truck up to a house with blue shutters and American flags. It takes him just 38 seconds to pump 50 gallons. In rural Aroostook County, median household income is $54,400, some $22,000 less than the state median. About 16% of all residents and 12% of seniors live in poverty. Jobs often revolve around trucking, logging and farming. When someone can’t afford heat, they call nonprofit organization Avec Community Action. In 2025, Avec got almost 8,000 home energy assistance applications from families in northern Maine and distributed more than $3 million in aid. Its small staff is under remarkable strain. The organization is responsible for Aroostook plus two nearby counties. There are 20 people processing thousands of applications for one-third of the state. By late September, staffers had 500 voicemails to return. Heidi Rackliffe, Avec’s chief program officer, was bringing her team in on weekends to call everybody back. “They rely on these programs,” Rackliffe said of Avec’s customers, “because that’s how they survive.” Jason Parent, Avec’s CEO, plays a voicemail from a resident who recently paid $500 to fill her tank. “Anyway, Jason, I’m really, really struggling. I’m still working at the age of 80 to try to make ends meet. Could you please call me today so that the anxiety doesn’t kick in too much?” Down the hall, Greta Power handles a growing stack of applications from middle-class families seeking help for the first time. Power keeps apples and mini 3 Musketeers in her office, knowing people skip meals to buy fuel. She gets angry thinking about last winter, when the longest government shutdown in American history delayed federal fuel funds for over a month. Then, Avec had to triage 80- and 90-year-olds most in need. “I cannot believe this is the United States,” Power said. STREAMING NOW: What happens when hard work is no longer enough? Priced Out in America follows families trapped in the affordability crisis, revealing structural forces that have profoundly and permanently reshaped the US economy. People were calling for emergency deliveries weeks before funds were available. Others made too much money for low-income programs or exhausted their one-time benefits with months of winter still to go. Intake appointments for heating aid were already booking out into February. Maine’s senior citizens on fixed incomes are among the hardest hit. The state has the nation’s oldest population – 23% of residents are 65 and up. Ruth Munson, 73, called Avec in late September. Her kerosene tank was almost out, and she needed an emergency fill-up. The chill was slipping through the cracks in her windows and warps in her 48-year-old trailer. Munson and her husband live off a combined $1,993 a month in Social Security and had been getting Avec’s help for decades. A wooden plaque on the wall said “The Munson Estate,” but the only luxury she bought was cable. High prices, she said, felt like “hell on wheels.” ‘Where are they gonna go?’ Bates keeps sending trucks to the customers who are behind on payments. He isn’t sure how much longer he can manage. Bates could retire and spend more time making maple syrup with his grandson. The shed behind his home is practically a science lab, full of jugs and evaporators and gallons of sap. But retirement also means selling all eight of his trucks and laying off workers. And what about his customers? Larger fuel dealers would never excuse so much debt, he said. “Where are they gonna go?” That question keeps Michael Fawcett buzzing around the Wytopitlock Food Pantry. He’d found “Pitlock” on the map 25 years ago, when he left Las Vegas in search of cheap land. Now, he leads a group of volunteers who dole out fresh produce, pasta, eggs and more every few weeks. He hoped to give his community some “margin,” he said. Almost all of the pantry’s customers are seniors, and there’s was a waitlist with a dozen more. Fawcett scraped together donations and runs the pantry without pay. He crisscrosses the town collecting bottles and cans for the 5 cent deposit. Sometimes his haul yields an extra $25. But the pantry is about $2,000 in the red every year. Insurance on the pantry truck: $1,100. Fuel: $950 and rising. Cleaning supplies, produce bags and other basics: $500. Doreen Crawford raised six children in Wytopitlock while her husband worked in trucking. Sometimes they had enough to get by; sometimes not. The 91-year-old has been coming to the pantry for at least 15 years. Crawford managed to lock in a price with her fuel vendor – $4.29 a gallon from September to May. But she was still sleeping without heat, preferring to “snuggle right down in there.” In the fall, she flicks on the heater for a few hours each morning, “just enough to take the chill out.” Sho Magby, 50, was already cold as she circled through the pantry and considered a small supermarket cake. She hadn’t taken off her grey beanie. She said she’d be out of firewood in the next few days. Her heating assistance appointment was over a month out. “I mean, I could use my oven,” Magby said. Staring down the months ahead, Bates hopes to keep people from making such a choice. Surely, the sprawling global market would eventually grant some relief. A bubble would burst. The price would drop. “I’ll grind through, probably, this winter,” Bates said. He isn’t counting on the midterms to change much of anything. Bates voted for Trump multiple times but said he doesn’t agree with everything the president has done. That’s typical around these parts, which Trump carried in 2024 by around 26 points. “We vote Republican because it’s like the lesser of the two evils,” Bates said. “I don’t look at the Republican Party as my savior or anything. Because they’re not.” He tallies the gallons he’s bought in the last few days. He counts how long it would take to pay it off. He keeps driving.

articles.title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Q2 results: Consolidated net profit jumps 26% to Rs 5,645 crore; margins narrow
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Kotak Mahindra Bank on Saturday reported a 26 per cent increase in consolidated net profit to Rs 5,645 crore for the September quarter of FY27,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Kotak Mahindra Bank on Saturday reported a 26 per cent increase in consolidated net profit to Rs 5,645 crore for the September quarter of FY27, compared with Rs 4,468 crore in the same period last year, as higher income and a decline in provisions supported earnings.The private sector lender's standalone net profit rose 29 per cent year-on-year to Rs 4,212 crore from Rs 3,253 crore.The bank also reported an improvement in asset quality during the quarter. Its gross non-performing assets (GNPA) ratio declined to 1.04 per cent from 1.39 per cent a year earlier, while the net NPA ratio fell to 0.24 per cent from 0.32 per cent.Fresh loan slippages decreased to Rs 1,230 crore from Rs 1,629 crore in the corresponding quarter last year. Provisions and contingencies were also lower, falling 15 per cent to Rs 803 crore.Additionally, it reported that its net interest income (NII) increased 16 per cent to Rs 8,459 crore from Rs 7,311 crore a year ago. Operating profit climbed 21 per cent to Rs 6,382 crore, while fees and services income grew 21 per cent to Rs 2,926 crore.The bank recorded a 25 per cent rise in net advances to Rs 5,77,295 crore as of September 30, 2026. Total deposits increased 23 per cent to Rs 6,51,491 crore.However, a significant part of this growth was linked to funds mobilised through the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) scheme. Excluding FCNR(B)-related loans and the portfolio acquired from Kotak Mahindra Investments, advances grew 19 per cent. Deposit growth stood at 13 per cent after excluding FCNR(B) deposits.Despite the increase in income, the bank witnessed pressure on its lending margins. Net interest margin (NIM) declined to 4.31 per cent from 4.54 per cent in the year-ago quarter and 4.53 per cent in the preceding quarter.The bank attributed the moderation largely to the mobilisation of around Rs 55,344 crore in FCNR(B) deposits under the Reserve Bank of India's concessional swap facility. It also disbursed loans worth approximately Rs 16,110 crore through its international branches under the arrangement.The inflows affected the bank's deposit mix, with its current account and savings account (CASA) ratio falling to 38.2 per cent from 42.3 per cent a year earlier. Excluding FCNR(B) deposits, the ratio stood at 41.8 per cent.Managing director and CEO Ashok Vaswani said the bank expects its net interest margins to remain stable during the rest of the financial year. While the deployment of funds raised through the FCNR(B) scheme could weigh on margins, the impact is expected to be offset by RBI rate hikes, given that around 60 per cent of the bank's loan book is linked to the repo rate.The bank's capital adequacy ratio stood at 21.9 per cent as of September 30, 2026, with its Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio at 21.4 per cent.You use AI every day.
